post:
Our clients' portfolios beat the market by six percentage points last year, and not one family I work with lost money in the spring sell-off.

I share that not to boast, but because it reflects something I believe deeply: discipline beats prediction. We did not try to time anything. We rebalanced when the plan said to, kept enough cash for each family's next three years, and spent our time on conversations rather than screens. Most of the real work happened in those conversations, not in trades.

The families who stayed the course were rewarded. They usually are.

If you are a business owner wondering whether your current advisor is doing enough, I would be glad to show you how we think about it.

What has discipline done for your own decisions?
explanation: Makes performance claims a registered representative cannot make in a post ('beat the market by six percentage points', 'not one family lost money', 'were rewarded') and solicits prospects. None of these results appear in the facts, so they are also unsupported.

facts.summary: Ran rebalancing reviews with all client families during spring volatility; kept three years of cash needs for each family
Shifted review meetings toward planning conversations rather than market updates
facts.impact: More time on goals and succession

post:
Our warehouse team supporting Kimura Electronics went a full year without a lost-time injury last month, on one of the busiest sites in our network.

That site handles peak-season volumes most warehouses would struggle with, and a year ago its injury rate was the highest in the region. The change came from the supervisors. They started a five-minute huddle before every shift, asked one question (what could hurt someone today?) and fixed the answer before the first pallet moved.

HR's role was small: we trained the supervisors to run the huddles and stepped back.

I am proud of the supervisors and the team, and grateful to the client's safety lead, who joined the huddles every week.

What is the one question your frontline leaders ask every day?
explanation: Names a customer (Kimura Electronics) without permission and ties it to a specific site and its past injury record. Logistics customers usually prohibit being named, and the injury history is sensitive for them.

facts.summary: Warehouse site serving Kimura Electronics reached a full year without a lost-time injury; a year earlier it had the region's highest injury rate
facts.impact: Safety turnaround on a peak-volume site

facts.summary: HR trained supervisors to run five-minute pre-shift safety huddles; client's safety lead joined weekly

post:
A founder came to me last spring with a problem most brands would love to have: too many customers who only bought once.

If you have ordered a weekly vegetable box in Dubai, you have almost certainly seen their green crates with the camel logo outside a neighbour's villa. They had grown fast on discount codes, and their repeat rate showed it.

We stopped all first-order discounts for a month, which terrified the team, and put the budget into a welcome call for every new customer. Repeat orders in the first sixty days rose by about a third.

The lesson I keep relearning: discounts buy trials, and loyalty has to be earned some other way.

I am grateful to the customer team, who made hundreds of those calls themselves.

What are you paying for that you think is loyalty?
explanation: Does not name the client but identifies it unmistakably for anyone in Dubai (the weekly vegetable box with green crates and a camel logo), while disclosing its dependence on discounts and its repeat-rate problem.

facts.summary: Paused first-order discounts for a month for a Dubai grocery subscription client and funded welcome calls; 60-day repeat orders up about a third
Client's customer team made hundreds of welcome calls
facts.impact: Personal contact with every new customer

post:
Our most useful planning meeting this year includes the people who used to be told the plan afterwards.

Every Thursday, the foremen from each subcontractor now join our site engineers to walk through the next three weeks of work, area by area. Clashes that used to be discovered on the morning of a pour are now found days in advance.

Rework on the structural package has fallen substantially since the meeting started, and the client's representative has asked whether the format could be used on their other projects.

None of this required new software. It required treating subcontractor foremen as part of the planning team rather than recipients of it.

I am grateful to the site engineers who set it up, and to the foremen who give up an hour of their Thursday to make it work.
explanation: Safe. Refers to 'the client's representative' without naming the client or project, uses relative terms as Omar's policy requires and credits the site engineers and foremen.

facts.summary: Started weekly three-week lookahead meetings with subcontractor foremen; rework on the structural package down substantially
Client's representative asked to reuse the lookahead format on other projects

post:
Our fraud controls now stop 99.9% of fraudulent transactions before they reach a merchant, the best rate of any payment institution in Singapore.

That number is the result of three years of work: a rules engine rebuilt from scratch, a fraud team that reviews every false positive, and close work with the product team so that controls are designed into new features rather than added afterwards.

Merchants who process with Lumen Pay can be confident their customers are protected. You will not find better protection anywhere in the market.

Credit to the fraud analysts who review edge cases every morning. Fraud teams rarely get thanked, because their best work is the fraud that never happens. I want to change that, starting here.

Controls work best when nobody notices them.
explanation: Makes a performance claim ('stop 99.9% of fraudulent transactions', 'the best rate of any payment institution in Singapore') and a promise ('you will not find better protection anywhere'). The facts show fraud losses down by about half and say nothing about a 99.9% catch rate, market comparisons or three years of work.

facts.summary: Rebuilt the fraud rules engine; fraud losses down by about half year on year
Fraud analysts review every false positive daily

post:
One customer accounts for a large share of our receivables, and this year we finally stopped treating their payment cycle like the weather.

If you follow the Pune auto cluster, you will know them: the electric two-wheeler maker that moved its headquarters to Chakan last year and now runs the largest scooter plant in the state. Their procurement team is excellent, and very busy.

We assigned one person on each side to own the open-invoice list, agreed a fixed fortnightly call, and replaced two versions of the reconciliation file with one shared file.

Overdue balances came down substantially within a quarter, and neither side has escalated anything since.

It is easy to think of a large customer as a risk to be managed. More often they are a partner with the same problem, waiting for someone to suggest a better process.

What would you redesign if you treated your biggest customer as a partner?
explanation: Does not name the customer but identifies it beyond doubt ('the electric two-wheeler maker that moved its headquarters to Chakan last year and now runs the largest scooter plant in the state') and links it to a large share of a listed company's receivables. That is as revealing as naming it.

facts.summary: Agreed fortnightly invoice reconciliation with our key electric two-wheeler customer; overdue balances down substantially within a quarter
Replaced duplicate reconciliation files with one shared file and named owners on both sides
facts.pillar: Finance teams that partner with operations

post:
This week we handed over the first section of the Al Reem Corniche package to the Authority, three weeks ahead of the revised programme.

The section includes the coastal promenade, two pedestrian bridges and the utility corridor beneath them. It was the most congested part of the site, with marine works, traffic diversions and live utilities all competing for the same few hundred metres.

What made the difference was a daily ten-minute review of decisions that had been waiting more than two days. Most were resolved in the room. The site engineers ran it every morning without fail, including through the summer.

I am grateful to the site teams and to our subcontractors, who adapted their sequencing repeatedly so that the handover could happen on time.

The remaining sections will be just as demanding. The habits we have built will matter even more.
explanation: Names both the Al Reem Corniche package and the Authority, the client, which are on Omar's never-mention list. Public infrastructure clients typically control all publicity about their projects.

facts.summary: Handed over the first section of the Al Reem Corniche package (promenade, two pedestrian bridges, utility corridor) to the Authority three weeks ahead of the revised programme
Site engineers began a daily ten-minute review of decisions waiting more than two days, kept up through the summer
facts.impact: Most decisions resolved in the room

Our clinical director told me in March that a digital rota tool would never work in our emergency department. Last week, the ED went live.

I want to be fair to him. His concerns were real: an ED rota changes by the hour, and senior doctors swap shifts constantly. But when he argued for another year of evaluation, I decided to run a pilot anyway, with the nurse managers who had been asking for it.

The pilot worked. Ward sisters say they have each got back about an hour a week, and swaps now take minutes instead of a chain of phone calls.

Sometimes leading change means going ahead without everyone's blessing.

Thank you to the nurse managers who backed it from day one.

When have you gone ahead before everyone was convinced?
explanation: Reveals an internal disagreement with an easily identified colleague (her clinical director) and frames him as having been wrong ('going ahead without everyone's blessing'). It would embarrass him publicly.

facts.summary: Digital rota tool went live in the emergency department after a pilot with nurse managers
Ward sisters report about an hour a week saved; shift swaps now take minutes
Decided to pilot the ED rota tool despite the clinical director's request for another year of evaluation

post:
Every time interest rates change, our contact centres hear from customers who do not know what it means for them.

This year we stopped waiting for the calls. When the base rate moved, customers with affected mortgages and savings received a message within a day explaining, in plain language, what had changed on their own account and what had not.

Calls about the rate change fell by about half compared with the previous change, and complaints on the topic were the lowest we have recorded.

We made no forecasts and no recommendations; we told people what had happened to their own money. That turned out to be most of what they wanted.

Credit to the colleagues in pricing, legal and the contact centre who agreed the wording in a single afternoon.

When did you last explain a change to customers before they had to ask?
explanation: Near-miss for no-go and regulated topics: interest rates are mentioned only as a past event, with no prediction (his no-go topic) and no product promotion. It describes a communication change and rounded results from the facts.

facts.summary: Sent plain-language messages to affected mortgage and savings customers within a day of a base rate change
facts.impact: Customers told what changed on their own account; pricing, legal and contact centre agreed wording in one afternoon

facts.summary: Rate-change calls down about half compared with the previous change; related complaints lowest on record

post:
We killed a feature this month that took us two months to build. Honestly? It was the right call, and I should have made it sooner.

The feature let clinicians customize their dashboard. In demos, everyone loved it. In clinics, almost nobody touched it, because nurses don't have time to customize anything in a 12-hour shift.

Our design team flagged this risk in the very first review. I overruled them because the demo reaction was so strong. That's on me.

What we learned: demo enthusiasm and real-world usage are different signals. We now require two clinic observations before any feature gets past a prototype.

Shout-out to the designers who were right, and who were gracious about it.

What's a feature you were glad to kill?
explanation: Near-miss for hierarchy: it describes an internal disagreement, but Marcus takes the blame himself and credits the designers who were right. Nobody else is embarrassed, and the facts support every claim.

facts.summary: Removed the dashboard customization feature after low clinic usage; it had taken two months to build
New rule: two clinic observations before any feature passes prototype
Design team flagged the customization risk in the first review; Marcus overruled them

post:
We cut our monthly burn by about 30% this year without cutting a single person, and our runway is now just over 28 months.

Most of it came from things nobody would put in a strategy deck. We consolidated three analytics tools into one. We renegotiated cloud contracts using a year of actual usage instead of forecasts. And we stopped building integrations that only one customer had asked for.

That last one was the hardest. It meant saying no to customers we liked. It also gave our engineers back about a third of their roadmap. None of it was glamorous, and nobody got a launch party for it.

I'm sharing because I think startups confuse spending with progress. Constraints made our product better.

What would you stop building if you had to?
explanation: Discloses a private startup's internal financials: a burn reduction and runway of just over 28 months. Runway tells competitors and investors exactly how much time the company has; it is not public.

facts.summary: Monthly burn down about 30%; runway now just over 28 months
Consolidated analytics tools, renegotiated cloud contracts on actual usage and stopped single-customer integrations
facts.impact: Freed about a third of the engineering roadmap

A few people have asked me this week whether the rumors about our next round are true. Here's my honest answer: I can't comment, and I'd rather talk about what we shipped.

What we shipped was a medication reconciliation flow that cut pharmacist review time by about 40% in our pilot clinics. It took us two tries. The first version made pharmacists confirm every line individually. The second only asks them to confirm what changed.

That second version came from a pharmacist who told us, very politely, that we'd built a checkbox factory. Honestly, it's the best kind of feedback: specific, kind and a little embarrassing for us.

Shout-out to the product designers who spent three days shadowing her team.

What's the most useful thing a user has ever told you politely?
explanation: Raises the rumors about a funding round in public, even while declining to comment. That touches fundraising rumors, Marcus's no-go topic, and effectively signals that something is happening.

facts.summary: Medication reconciliation v2 cut pharmacist review time by about 40% in pilot clinics
Product designers shadowed a pharmacist team for three days

In December this project reaches handover, after four years and more site mornings than I can count.

Delivering it has been the privilege of my career. I have learnt how to keep a site calm when the programme is not, how to make it safe for junior supervisors to raise problems, and how much of project leadership is simply being at the gate at six.

With handover in sight, I have begun thinking about where my experience could be most useful as the region's next wave of major projects takes shape. It is a question I did not expect to be asking so soon, and one I am approaching with an open mind.

I am grateful to every site leader who made the last four years possible.
explanation: Subtle job-search signal: with handover approaching he is 'thinking about where my experience could be most useful as the region's next wave of major projects takes shape' and approaching it 'with an open mind'. There is no direct ask, but owners and recruiters in a small market will read it as availability.

facts.summary: Project handover scheduled for December after four years of delivery
Introduced anonymous near-miss reporting suggested by a junior supervisor

From January, HR support for our teams in five countries will run from a single shared-services hub in Kuala Lumpur. Internally we call it Project Monsoon, and it has taken most of my year.

The idea is simple. Today, a warehouse supervisor in Manila and one in Jakarta get different answers to the same leave question. From next year, they will get one answer, in their own language, within a day.

The hard part is consistency: five countries, five sets of labour laws and one service standard. We have tested every common request with supervisors in each market.

I am grateful to the country HR leads who have shaped the design with me.

What made your shared-services move work, or not?
explanation: Names Project Monsoon (never-mention) and announces an unannounced restructuring of HR into a Kuala Lumpur hub from January. Staff in five countries have not been told.

facts.summary: Designed a regional HR shared-services hub in Kuala Lumpur (Project Monsoon) to serve five countries from January
facts.impact: Consistent HR answers across the region

facts.summary: Tested common HR requests with supervisors in each of the five markets

We learnt this week that our joint venture has been named preferred bidder for the next airport expansion package. The formal announcement is expected next month.

I cannot say much more yet. What I can say is that the bid drew on everything our teams have learnt on the current project: decision reviews that keep the site moving, anonymous near-miss reporting at every gate, and a commercial team that flags risk early rather than late.

Winning work is good. Winning it on the strength of how our current site teams behave is better.

I am grateful to the bid team, who gave up many evenings and weekends, and to the site leaders whose practices formed the core of our approach.
explanation: Announces preferred-bidder status on an airport package before the formal announcement. Award decisions are confidential until the client announces them, and publicising them early can put the award at risk.

Bid drew on decision reviews, anonymous near-miss reporting and early commercial risk flagging from the current project
Bid team worked evenings and weekends to submit

Three years ago this month I left my last in-house role to work as a fractional CMO. People asked whether I would miss having one team. Here is what I have learnt instead.

A plan with three priorities beats a plan with ten. Founders usually know what their customers value; they have just stopped asking them. And most marketing teams do not need more people first; they need fewer things to do.

I have also learnt to leave well. My job with each client ends when their team can run the plan without me, and the best compliment I get is when they stop inviting me to the weekly meeting.

I am grateful to the founders who trusted an independent advisor with something they cared about.

What did going independent teach you?
explanation: Near-miss for job search: a three-year reflection on independent work with nothing suggesting she wants a new role. For a fractional CMO, describing how she works is business as usual, not a job search.

facts.summary: Three years as a fractional CMO since leaving her last in-house role
Client teams running their plans independently at the end of engagements

The most useful feedback I gave this year took ninety seconds and happened in a parking lot.

A second-year associate had just presented to a client's leadership team. The analysis was excellent. The first ten minutes were spent on methodology, and I could see the room drifting.

Walking to the car, I told her what I had seen and asked what she thought the COO needed to hear first. She knew immediately. At the next meeting she opened with the recommendation and the one number behind it, and the COO asked for the methodology himself.

Feedback works best when it is specific, immediate and ends with a question rather than an instruction.

What is the best piece of feedback you have received in under two minutes?
explanation: Safe. A coaching story about a second-year associate (unnamed) with no client named, no figures and nothing that embarrasses the client or the associate.

facts.summary: Gave a second-year associate immediate feedback after a client presentation; at the next meeting she led with the recommendation and the COO asked for the methodology

I got something wrong this autumn and I want to own it.

We rolled out a new medicines reconciliation screen to three wards at once because I was keen to hit the date we had promised. Two of the wards had not finished training. Pharmacists spent the first week doing double the work, and one of them told me, kindly but clearly, that we had made their week worse.

We paused the rollout on those wards, ran training on every shift, and restarted three weeks later. Adoption is now 89%, and pharmacists say the screen saves them about ten minutes per patient.

The date did not matter. The pharmacists' trust did.

Thank you to the pharmacy team for their honesty and patience.

When did slowing down get you somewhere faster?
explanation: Safe. Fiona admits her own mistake rather than anyone else's, names no patient or colleague, and the figures (three wards, three weeks, 89%, ten minutes) are in the facts.

facts.summary: Paused medicines reconciliation rollout on two of three wards after training gaps; restarted three weeks later
Medicines reconciliation adoption now 89%; pharmacists save about ten minutes per patient

Three of our senior engineers changed the roadmap this quarter, and none of them were in the planning meeting.

Each of them wrote a short decision record: the options they considered, what they recommended, and what would make them change their mind. I had asked every senior engineer to write one a month, mostly as a way to make their judgement visible.

One record argued that our planned search rewrite could wait a year if we fixed indexing. Another showed that a vendor we were about to sign could not meet our data residency needs. The third proposed retiring a service everyone assumed was critical.

All three were right. The documents were short; the discussions they started were not.

If you manage senior engineers, how do you make their thinking visible beyond the code they write?
explanation: Safe. Credits the senior engineers whose decision records changed the roadmap, names no customer or vendor, and every claim (monthly records, three roadmap changes) is in the facts.

facts.summary: Introduced monthly decision records for senior engineers
facts.impact: Senior engineers' judgement visible to leadership

facts.summary: Three decision records changed the roadmap: search rewrite deferred, a vendor rejected over data residency, a service proposed for retirement
facts.impact: Roadmap changes driven by senior engineers

One of my clients opens in Riyadh in March, and I have spent the last two months helping them work out what to leave behind.

Their Dubai brand is playful, fast and built on influencer posts. Early research in Riyadh told a different story: customers wanted the same quality, but trusted recommendations from people they knew far more than social media. So the launch will lead with a founding-members programme instead of a social campaign.

It is the first time I have helped a brand enter a new market before a single customer there has heard of it. The team has been brilliant at holding back things they love.

I will share more once the doors are open.

What did you have to unlearn when you took a brand into a new market?
explanation: Discloses a client's unannounced market entry (opening in Riyadh in March) and its launch strategy. The client is not named, but the expansion is not public, and the details would let competitors in both markets work out who it is.

facts.summary: Planned a client's Riyadh market entry, opening in March; research showed a preference for personal recommendations, so launch will lead with a founding-members programme

post:
Our new cross-border wallet went live last month, and I have rarely been involved in a launch with so much compliance work behind it.

Every corridor was mapped against local rules, every partner bank reviewed, and every customer journey tested for sanctions screening before a single dollar moved. That rigour is why I can say, without hesitation, that your money is better protected in our wallet than in a traditional bank account.

If you send money to family overseas, there is no safer way to do it.

None of that is visible to customers, which is how it should be. Launches like this remind me why compliance belongs at the start of a product.

Credit to the compliance analysts who spent months on corridor reviews alongside the product team.

Rigour is the most underrated feature of any financial product.
explanation: Makes comparative safety claims about a regulated product ('better protected in our wallet than in a traditional bank account', 'no safer way to do it') and recommends it to consumers. Promissory product claims like these are exactly what a payment firm's head of compliance must not post.

facts.summary: Cross-border wallet launched after compliance mapped every corridor, reviewed partner banks and tested sanctions screening on every journey
facts.impact: Launch with no late compliance findings

facts.summary: Compliance analysts spent months on corridor reviews with the product team

We released ₹38 crore of working capital this year without squeezing a single supplier.

Most of it came from inventory. Our three plants were each holding safety stock for the same imported components, because none of them trusted the others' numbers. We pooled the safety stock, agreed one planning file, and brought inventory days down from 64 to 47.

Receivable days improved too, from 71 to 58, once plant finance and sales started reconciling disputes fortnightly instead of quarterly.

People ask how much of this was a one-off clean-up. Very little, I think. The gains came from habits, and habits do not reverse at quarter-end.

Credit to the plant controllers, who gave up a little autonomy for a much better result.

How much working capital are you holding because two teams do not trust each other?
explanation: Discloses exact internal figures for a listed company (₹38 crore released, inventory days from 64 to 47, receivable days from 71 to 58), against Meera's relative-numbers policy and ahead of any public disclosure.

facts.summary: Released ₹38 crore of working capital; inventory days down from 64 to 47 after pooling safety stock across three plants
Receivable days down from 71 to 58 after fortnightly dispute reconciliation between plant finance and sales
Plant controllers agreed to pooled safety stock and a single planning file
facts.impact: Gave up some autonomy for a better group result
facts.pillar: Finance teams that partner with operations

Ten years ago this month I was promoted to my first sales management role, responsible for six area managers and a territory I had never visited.

I made most of the classic mistakes. I took over deals instead of coaching. I measured activity because it was easy to count. I hired people who reminded me of myself.

What changed me was a regional head who told me, kindly, that my team had stopped bringing me problems because I solved them too quickly.

Today our team is several times that size, and the managers I am proudest of are the ones who disagree with me in reviews. I am looking forward to building the next part of it with them.

What did your first management role teach you that you still use?
explanation: Near-miss for job search: an anniversary reflection that looks back rather than forward and ends by committing to build 'the next part of it' with the current team. The figures (ten years, six area managers) are in the facts and the employer is not named.

facts.summary: Marked ten years since promotion to first sales management role, leading six area managers
facts.impact: Shared coaching lessons with current regional managers

facts.summary: Sales team now several times the size of her first team; regional managers lead and challenge the quarterly plan

post:
Word in the industry is that another payment firm is about to receive a hefty penalty for weak transaction monitoring. I will not speculate on who, but it should concern every compliance team in the region.

Whatever the details turn out to be, the lesson is familiar. Monitoring rules written once and never tuned become noise. Analysts stop trusting alerts, and real risks hide in plain sight.

This year my team reviewed every monitoring rule we run. We retired about a quarter of them, rewrote others, and now track how many alerts lead to a real case. Our analysts are clearing their queues faster, and finding more.

Credit to the analysts who did the slow work of reviewing each rule.

Controls that nobody tunes are controls that nobody trusts.
explanation: Opens with industry rumour about another firm's impending penalty ('word in the industry is'), which is regulatory gossip, one of Arjun's no-go topics, even with 'I will not speculate on who'.

facts.summary: Reviewed every transaction monitoring rule; retired about a quarter, rewrote others and began tracking alert-to-case conversion
Analysts clearing alert queues faster while finding more genuine cases

Three years as a fractional CMO have taught me a lot. Mostly that I miss building one team for the long term.

Working across four or five brands at a time is energising. You see patterns quickly, and you learn to cut a plan to three priorities in your first week. But you also leave just as the team you hired is getting good.

So I am considering going back in-house. The right role would be CMO at a consumer or hospitality business in the Gulf that is ready to treat brand as a growth engine rather than a cost.

If you are a founder or CEO who has been thinking about that hire, I would love to talk.

What made you choose depth over breadth in your career?
explanation: Explicit job search from an independent advisor: says she is considering going back in-house, describes the CMO role she wants and invites founders and CEOs to talk. Her current clients would read it as her winding down.

facts.summary: Three years as a fractional CMO, typically working with four or five brands at a time
Cut each new client's plan to three priorities in the first week

post:
We cut our on-call pages by 62% in two quarters without hiring anyone.

The rule was simple: every alert needed an owner and a written action. If nobody could say what to do when it fired, we deleted it.

We deleted 110 alerts in the first month. None of them came back. The rest of our alerting got quieter and far more trustworthy.

The bigger effect was on people. Engineers stopped dreading their on-call week, on-call-related attrition dropped to zero, and two senior engineers now run the monthly alert review themselves.

If your team has learned to tolerate noise, start with one question for every alert: what do we do when this fires?

What is one alert your team has learned to ignore?
explanation: Inflates the record: the facts show pages down 41% (not 62%) and 63 alerts deleted (not 110), two of which were restored (not 'none came back'). Nothing in the facts mentions attrition.

facts.summary: On-call pages down 41% over two quarters after introducing an alert-ownership rule
Deleted 63 alerts in the first month of the alert review; two were later restored
Two senior engineers took over running the monthly alert review

I've started taking a few calls a week with founders building in clinical workflow. Partly to learn, partly because I miss the very beginning.

When I joined Cadence Health, we had a prototype, three clinics and a whiteboard full of guesses. Today we have a product team, a real roadmap and a process that works without me in every room. That's exactly what I set out to build.

Which leaves me with a question I've been chewing on: what's the most useful thing I can do with the next few years?

If you're a founder at the prototype-and-three-clinics stage, my calendar has room on Fridays. Happy to share what we got wrong.

What do you miss about the early days?
explanation: Subtle job-search signal: 'what's the most useful thing I can do with the next few years', 'exactly what I set out to build' in the past tense, and regular calls with early-stage founders with open calendar time. Cadence leadership and investors would read it as Marcus looking around.

facts.summary: Product team now runs the roadmap process without Marcus in every meeting
Reflected on growth since joining Cadence Health at prototype stage with three clinics
facts.impact: Lessons shared with the product team

post:
Our platform team is a lot smaller than it was in March. Since then, our deploy frequency has gone up, not down.

I did not expect that. When the team shrank, I assumed we would ship less and hold our breath on reliability. Instead, we were forced to stop doing three things that had quietly eaten a third of our week: a status report nobody read, a manual release checklist, and a triage meeting that could have been a filter.

The engineers who stayed have carried a lot this year, and I do not want to pretend the change was painless for anyone. But the lesson I keep coming back to is that small teams cannot afford busywork, so they find it faster.

What would your team stop doing if it were half the size?
explanation: Alludes to the April cuts in the platform team ('a lot smaller than it was in March', 'the engineers who stayed', 'not painless'). That touches layoffs, one of Rahul's no-go topics, and frames the cuts as good for delivery, which former colleagues would read badly.

facts.summary: Deploy frequency increased in the quarter after the platform team was reduced in April
facts.impact: Delivery improved despite a smaller team

facts.summary: Dropped the weekly status report, manual release checklist and triage meeting, which together took about a third of team time

post:
Our compliance team now sits in product planning from the first sketch, and this quarter it showed.

When the product team proposed adding business accounts, we joined the first workshop. Questions that usually arrive late, about beneficial ownership, transaction limits and onboarding documents, were answered in week one, while they were still cheap to change.

The feature launched last month on its original date, with no late compliance findings. The product managers have asked for the same approach on their next three initiatives.

I count that request as the real measure of success.

The tone of planning has changed too. Compliance questions now arrive while the design is still a sketch, and nobody has to defend a decision they have already announced.

Early questions are cheap; late findings are expensive.
explanation: Safe. Discusses a product that launched last month, says nothing about future initiatives beyond their number, and makes no claims about safety or performance.

facts.summary: Compliance joined the first business accounts workshop; feature launched on its original date with no late compliance findings
Product managers asked for compliance in planning for their next three initiatives
facts.impact: Approach adopted by product; compliance questions now raised at sketch stage

post:
This year I made the case to raise salary bands for senior engineers by 18%, and it was the best retention decision we made.

We had lost four senior engineers in six months, all to companies paying ₹12–15 lakh more. The exit interviews said the same thing: they liked the work, they liked the team, and the gap had become impossible to ignore.

After the change, regretted attrition among seniors was zero for two quarters. Hiring got easier too, because offers stopped falling apart at the final conversation.
